title: Model Drift Objection Battlecard - Draft
body:
Purpose and audience:
- Short: give sellers and SEs a compact, technically-savvy script and evidence kit to handle "model drift" objections during pilot/POC and procurement conversations.
- Audience: sellers (SEs, AE), platform sellers, solutions engineers, and pilot owners.
- Scope: objections about accuracy/quality degradation over time, retraining cadence, and who owns monitoring and remediation. Not a deep ML engineering how-to.

Why this matters (customer language):
- "We love the model quality now, but what happens in 3–6 months when our data distribution shifts?"
- Drift fear kills pilots: customers often pause or add long review windows if drift feels uncontrollable.
- We want to reduce friction by converting fear into concrete controls: metrics, responsibilities, SLAs, and small experiments.

Top-level seller talking points (elevator):
1) Observability-first: Redwood can attach continuous quality signals to every route/version so you see early changes, not surprises.
2) Ownership model: we support either customer-owned monitors (recommended for sensitive domains) or Redwood-managed alerts tied to rollbacks and canary policies.
3) Safe rollouts: canaries + automatic fallback to a pinned, stable variant keep production stable while enabling model iteration.
4) Fast recovery: lineage, per-request metadata, and prompt/eval tracing let you isolate cause quickly.

Quick objection-response scripts (use conversationally):
- Objection: "We’re worried about model drift and silent quality loss."
  Response: "Totally fair. On Redwood you get continuous quality hooks out of the box — we can send threshold alerts when your evals degrade, run automatic canaries for new model versions, and fall back instantly to your certified variant. If you want, we’ll add your core prompt set for ongoing regression checks during the pilot."

- Objection: "Who maintains the monitors and acts on alerts?"
  Response: "We offer two flows: 1) Your team owns monitors (we provide APIs/export hooks to plug into Datadog/Prometheus), or 2) Redwood operates baseline guards as part of your Dedicated/Private plan and notifies your on-call with recommended actions and a rollback. For pilots, most customers prefer option 1 but we can run option 2 for the first 30 days."

- Objection: "Can we prove drift is happening and not just change in requirements?"
  Response: "Yes — we record per-request signals (prompt, context vector hash, model version, output token-level scores). Combined with your labeled checks, you can segment by input cohorts and isolate distributional shift vs label noise."

Evidence kit (what to show in a demo or deck):
- Live sample of a daily quality dashboard showing: avg. eval score, top failing prompts, cohort drift heatmap, and token-level latency/cost.
- Canary timeline: a simulated model release showing 0 -> 1% -> 10% traffic with automated A/B drift checks and auto-fallback at configured threshold.
- Alert to incident flow: sample notification (Slack/PagerDuty), recommended runbook steps, and example rollback command (single-line in Console).

Technical appendix (short for SEs):
- Signals we surface: per-call embedding distance to reference distribution, language-model log-prob gap to baseline, perplexity surges, output hallucination heuristics (entity hallucination score), and custom eval metrics (customer-supplied).
- Integration points: Redwood exports events to S3/BigQuery, emits metrics to Prometheus, and can ship alerts to PagerDuty/Slack.
- Canary mechanics: split routing policies can target percent-of-requests and cohort-aware routing (by user segment, region, or prompt hash). Rollback is supported via an atomic route update with no downtime.

Pilot checklist (what to request from the prospect during discovery):
- Baseline: Provide a representative prompt set (50–200 canonical prompts) and 2–3 labeled examples per common failure mode.
- Labels: Who will label failures during pilot? (Customer ops or SE partnership).
- Success criteria: Define one primary metric (semantic-match F1 / BLEU-ish / human-acceptance %) and 2 secondary metrics (latency SLO, cost per 1k calls).
- Operational handoff: On-call contact, preferred alert channel, and decision threshold for auto-fallback during pilot.

Two short pilot patterns (scripted):
1) Low-trust pilot (fast safety):
- Start with 5% traffic to Redwood-hosted model variant + daily regression run on canonical prompts.
- Redwood will send daily digest + pager alert on >5% relative drop vs baseline.
- Rollback rule: automatic fallback at 10% drop or manual rollback option.
- Outcome: customer gets confidence, we gather label pairs.

2) High-trust pilot (platform-first):
- Dedicated environment with customer-managed monitors; 100% test traffic but gated by internal approvals.
- Weekly model swaps with gated canary.
- Outcome: faster scale to production after 2–4 weeks of monitoring.

Common customer risk patterns and seller playbook:
- Risk: No canonical prompts -> ask them to pull 50–100 common queries from logs and commit to labeling.
- Risk: No on-call -> offer Redwood-managed guardrails for first 30 days.
- Risk: Regulatory audit concerns -> emphasize Private deployment options, audit logs, and KMS integration.

Open questions for product/infra (notes to self):
- Can we add a one-click export for canonical prompt regression snapshots? (SE request)
- Is there an existing UI flow to show "most changed tokens by cohort"? If not, backlog candidate.
- Need example YAML snippet for auto-fallback policy to include in next demo kit.

Suggested collateral to attach for next SE enablement batch:
- Short 2-slide rapid demo: (1) Drift dashboard, (2) Canary timeline + rollback.
- 1-page cheat sheet for SEs: quick commands to create route canary, enable guard rails, and trigger manual rollback.
- Example eval set (anonymized) + Jupyter notebook for rolling drift analysis.

Metrics we recommend for negotiation (show to customer):
- Quality signal: % of canonical prompts passing acceptance threshold (primary).
- Drift detection latency: median time from distributional shift start to alert.
- Operational recovery time (MTTR): median time to rollback from alert.
- Cost: incremental token/compute cost for continuous evals (estimate per 1k calls).

Role play snippets (two-liners):
- SE -> Customer: "If we find drift, do you want us to pause the rollout or keep it live and notify? Most teams pick pause+notify for high-risk flows."
- Customer -> SE: "Will we lose performance if we enable continuous evals?" SE: "Minimal — continuous evals run on a sampling basis and we recommend sampling 1–5% of traffic for heavy checks. We can show the cost impact up-front."

Next steps (for AE/SE):
- Attach canonical prompt set to pilot kickoff doc.
- Agree on the primary metric, alerting threshold, and rollback rule in the pilot SOW.
- Schedule a 30-minute demo with ops+engineering to walk the dashboard and show a simulated canary failover.

Notes to include in final deck: keep language non-ML-jargon for buyer slide (C-level), include 1 concrete customer example (anonymized) where canary rollback prevented a production incident, and include explicit SLAs around rollback/response times if customer purchases Dedicated.

Unresolved items (for product/GTM sync):
- Example anonymized customer case study to include (need legal approval).
- Exact default thresholds for auto-fallback (product to confirm).

Slack threads / references: #se-pilot-onboarding, #gtm-ops, #prod-detection (tagging Diego & Sofia for input).

-- end of draft --

(Internal: this is meant to be a compact quick-read for sellers; convert to a 2-slide and 1-pager format after review.)
